subject: biology
title: When homeostasis fails
summary: How malfunctions in homeostatic control cause conditions such as type 1 diabetes, hyperthyroidism and disorders of water balance, explained step by step through the stimulus–response model.
body:
Homeostasis only works if every part of the stimulus–response pathway does its job. If a gland makes too little or too much of a hormone, or target cells stop responding, the variable drifts outside its tolerance range and the person becomes unwell. Studying these failures helps you understand normal homeostasis and explains why treatments such as insulin injections work.

## Think of it like this

### Type 1 and type 2 diabetes are like two ways a group chat can fail

Imagine the pancreas sends the message "take in glucose now!" to a group chat of muscle, fat and liver cells. In **type 1 diabetes**, the person who sends the message has been kicked out of the chat: the **beta cells** have been destroyed, so no **insulin** message is ever sent. In **type 2 diabetes**, the message is still being sent, but most of the group has the chat on mute, so they barely react. That is **insulin resistance**. Either way the job does not get done and blood glucose stays high (**hyperglycaemia**), but the fault is in a different place, so the fix is different.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a muted chat can be unmuted with one tap, but insulin resistance develops gradually and is managed (not instantly switched off) with lifestyle changes and medicines.

### Glucose in the urine is like buses after a big concert

After a normal gig, there are enough buses to get everyone home. In the kidney, the carrier proteins that reabsorb glucose from the filtrate are the buses, and normally every glucose molecule gets a ride back into the blood. After a huge concert, the buses fill up and people are left stranded at the stop. When blood glucose is very high, the carriers are all busy, so some glucose is left in the filtrate and ends up in the urine. Those "stranded" glucose molecules also hold water back in the filtrate, which is why people with untreated diabetes make lots of urine and feel very thirsty.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* buses come back for a second trip, but the filtrate keeps moving along the nephron, so glucose that is not reabsorbed the first time is simply lost in the urine.

### Graves' disease is like a heater wired straight into the wall

A normal heater is controlled by a thermostat: when the room gets warm, the thermostat cuts the power. That is **negative feedback**, like high **thyroxine** switching off **TSH**. In **Graves' disease**, it is as if someone wired the heater straight into the power point. The thermostat still turns down (TSH is low), but it makes no difference, because the **antibodies** keep switching the thyroid on directly. So thyroxine stays high and the **metabolic rate** stays up.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a heater just makes heat, but extra thyroxine affects almost every cell in the body, causing a fast heart rate, weight loss and nervousness as well as feeling hot.

### In real life

Many people with type 1 diabetes now wear a small sensor that tracks blood glucose and an insulin pump that delivers insulin under the skin, replacing the missing step in the pathway. Thyroxine needs iodine to be made, which is why most bread in Australia is made with iodised salt.

## Key ideas

### A framework for any malfunction

To explain any homeostatic disorder, ask: **which part of the pathway has failed?**

`stimulus → receptor → control centre → signal (nerve or hormone) → effector → response`

- **Receptor failure**: the change is not detected.
- **Control centre or gland failure**: too little hormone (**hyposecretion**) or too much (**hypersecretion**).
- **Effector or target cell failure**: hormone is present, but cells lack working receptors, so they do not respond.
- **Loss of feedback**: the signal no longer switches off when the variable returns to normal.

Once you know where the fault is, you can predict what happens to the variable and what the symptoms will be.

### Type 1 diabetes

**Type 1 diabetes** is an **autoimmune disease**: the immune system wrongly attacks the person's own cells. In this case it destroys the **beta cells** in the pancreatic islets. The fault is at the gland: little or no **insulin** is produced.

What follows, step by step:

1. After a meal, glucose is absorbed and blood glucose rises.
2. With no insulin, muscle and fat cells take up little glucose, and the liver does not store it as glycogen.
3. Blood glucose stays high. This is called **hyperglycaemia**.
4. Because nothing opposes it, glucagon effects continue and the liver keeps releasing glucose, making it worse.
5. The kidneys filter glucose into the nephron. Normally all of it is reabsorbed, but the carrier proteins that reabsorb glucose can only work so fast. When blood glucose is very high, some glucose stays in the filtrate and appears in the urine.
6. Glucose in the filtrate lowers its water concentration, so less water is reabsorbed by osmosis. The person produces large volumes of urine, becomes dehydrated and feels very thirsty.
7. Cells are starved of glucose even though blood glucose is high. They break down fats and proteins for energy, leading to weight loss and tiredness. Breaking down large amounts of fat can produce acidic **ketones**, which can lower blood pH dangerously.

**Treatment**: because the missing piece is the hormone, people with type 1 diabetes replace it with insulin injections or an insulin pump, monitor blood glucose, and match insulin doses to food and exercise. Too much insulin can cause **hypoglycaemia** (low blood glucose), which can cause shakiness, confusion and, if severe, loss of consciousness. Fast-acting sugar fixes this.

### Contrast: type 2 diabetes

In **type 2 diabetes**, the pancreas usually still makes insulin, at least at first, but target cells respond poorly to it. This is **insulin resistance**. The fault is at the target cells rather than the gland. The result is still high blood glucose, but the cause is different, so management is different too (often lifestyle changes and medicines that improve the response to insulin, with insulin added later if needed).

### Thyroid control and hyperthyroidism

The **thyroid gland** in the neck secretes **thyroxine** (also called T4), which raises the **metabolic rate** of most body cells: how fast they carry out reactions such as cellular respiration. Thyroxine needs iodine to be made.

Normal control uses negative feedback:

1. The hypothalamus releases **TRH** (thyrotropin-releasing hormone).
2. TRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release **TSH** (thyroid-stimulating hormone).
3. TSH stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine.
4. When thyroxine levels are high, it inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary, so less TRH and TSH are released, and thyroxine falls back.

**Hyperthyroidism** means too much thyroxine (hypersecretion). A common cause is **Graves' disease**, an autoimmune condition in which the body makes **antibodies** that bind to the TSH receptors on thyroid cells and activate them, just as TSH would. The key point is that these antibodies are not controlled by negative feedback. Even though high thyroxine lowers TSH from the pituitary, the antibodies keep stimulating the thyroid.

Symptoms follow from a raised metabolic rate:

- More heat production, so feeling hot and sweating; poor tolerance of heat.
- Faster heart rate.
- Weight loss despite a big appetite, because energy is used faster.
- Nervousness, shakiness and trouble sleeping.
- An enlarged thyroid (**goitre**), because the gland is constantly stimulated.

Treatments aim to reduce thyroxine output, for example with medicines that block thyroxine production, or by destroying or removing part of the thyroid (after which the person may need thyroxine tablets).

The opposite, **hypothyroidism** (too little thyroxine), causes a low metabolic rate: tiredness, feeling cold and weight gain.

### Disorders of water balance

Water balance depends on ADH (see the homeostasis lesson). Faults can occur at several points.

**Diabetes insipidus** (not related to blood glucose) has two forms:

- **Central** diabetes insipidus: the hypothalamus or pituitary does not make or release enough ADH. This is a gland fault.
- **Nephrogenic** diabetes insipidus: ADH is made, but kidney collecting duct cells do not respond to it, for example because their ADH receptors do not work. This is a target cell fault.

In both forms, collecting ducts stay poorly permeable to water, too little water is reabsorbed, and the person produces very large volumes of dilute urine. They become dehydrated, the blood becomes too concentrated and they feel extremely thirsty. Central diabetes insipidus can be treated with a synthetic form of ADH; nephrogenic cannot be fixed this way, because the problem is the response, not the hormone.

**Too much ADH** (sometimes called SIADH, syndrome of inappropriate ADH) is the reverse: too much water is reabsorbed, urine is small in volume and concentrated, and the blood becomes too dilute. Low salt concentration in the blood can make cells, including brain cells, swell with water by osmosis, causing headaches, confusion and, in severe cases, seizures.

**Dehydration** itself, such as from severe vomiting, diarrhoea or heavy sweating, can overwhelm normal control when water is lost faster than ADH and thirst can make up for.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: identifying the fault from hormone levels

Two patients both have high blood glucose. Patient X has very low insulin. Patient Y has high insulin.

1. Patient X: the pancreas is not producing insulin. The fault is at the gland, consistent with type 1 diabetes. Insulin injections should lower glucose.
2. Patient Y: insulin is being made, often in large amounts, but glucose is still high. The target cells are not responding: insulin resistance, consistent with type 2 diabetes.
3. Conclusion: the same symptom (hyperglycaemia) can come from faults at different points in the pathway.

### Example 2: Graves' disease and TSH

A patient has high thyroxine and very low TSH. Explain.

1. High thyroxine should feed back to the pituitary and reduce TSH. Low TSH shows this feedback is working.
2. Yet thyroxine is still high, so something other than TSH must be stimulating the thyroid.
3. In Graves' disease, antibodies bind to TSH receptors and activate thyroid cells. Feedback cannot switch off these antibodies.
4. Thyroxine stays high, raising metabolic rate and causing symptoms such as weight loss and a fast heart rate.

## Common mistakes

- Saying type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar. It is an autoimmune destruction of beta cells.
- Confusing diabetes insipidus with diabetes mellitus. Diabetes insipidus is about ADH and water, not glucose.
- Saying glucose in the urine means the kidney is not filtering. Glucose in urine means more glucose was filtered than the tubule could reabsorb.
- Thinking low TSH means the thyroid is underactive. In Graves' disease, TSH is low because high thyroxine suppresses it.
- Forgetting to link symptoms back to the mechanism (for example, high metabolic rate explains feeling hot).

## Exam tips

- Locate the fault in the stimulus–response pathway first, then explain the consequences in order.
- Use cause-and-effect chains with "so" or "therefore" linking each step.
- In data questions, compare hormone levels with the variable: a high variable with low hormone points to the gland; a high variable with high hormone points to the target cells.
- Explain why a treatment works by naming the missing or faulty step it replaces or corrects.

## Tips to remember

- **Find the broken link**: picture the stimulus–response pathway as a chain and ask which link snapped: receptor, gland (too much or too little hormone), target cells, or feedback.
- **Lock and key for diabetes**: type 1 = no key (beta cells destroyed, no insulin); type 2 = jammed lock (insulin present but target cells respond poorly).
- **Data rule**: high variable + low hormone → look at the gland; high variable + high hormone → look at the target cells.
- **Mellitus = honey, insipidus = tasteless**: diabetes mellitus is about glucose (sweet urine); diabetes insipidus is about ADH and water (large volumes of dilute urine).
- **Graves' disease = a doorbell jammed on**: the antibodies keep "pressing" the TSH receptors, ignoring negative feedback, so thyroxine stays high even though TSH is low.
- **Hyperthyroid = everything sped up**: hot, sweaty, fast heart, weight loss. Hypothyroid = everything slowed down: tired, cold, weight gain.

## Key terms

- **Hyposecretion** — a gland releasing too little hormone
- **Hypersecretion** — a gland releasing too much hormone
- **Autoimmune disease** — a disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells
- **Type 1 diabetes** — autoimmune destruction of beta cells, causing little or no insulin
- **Type 2 diabetes** — high blood glucose mainly due to target cells responding poorly to insulin
- **Insulin resistance** — reduced response of target cells to insulin
- **Hyperglycaemia** — blood glucose above the normal range
- **Hypoglycaemia** — blood glucose below the normal range
- **Thyroxine** — thyroid hormone that raises metabolic rate
- **TSH** — pituitary hormone that stimulates the thyroid
- **Hyperthyroidism** — overproduction of thyroxine
- **Graves' disease** — autoimmune condition in which antibodies activate TSH receptors
- **Goitre** — an enlarged thyroid gland
- **Diabetes insipidus** — condition in which too little ADH, or no response to it, causes large volumes of dilute urine

## Summary

- Homeostatic disorders happen when a part of the stimulus–response pathway fails.
- Type 1 diabetes: beta cells are destroyed, no insulin, so blood glucose stays high, with glucose in urine, thirst and weight loss.
- Type 2 diabetes differs: insulin is made but target cells respond poorly.
- Hyperthyroidism (often Graves' disease) raises metabolic rate because antibodies stimulate the thyroid outside negative feedback control.
- Diabetes insipidus (low ADH or no response) causes large volumes of dilute urine; too much ADH makes the blood too dilute.

questions.prompt: What is the cause of type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Target cells become resistant to insulin
options.B: The pituitary releases too little ADH
options.C: The immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells
options.D: The liver produces too much glycogen

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune: beta cells are destroyed so little or no insulin is made. Option A describes type 2 diabetes, the most common confusion.

questions.prompt: Which hormone is produced in excess in hyperthyroidism?
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism is hypersecretion of thyroxine by the thyroid gland. TSH is also involved in control, but it is thyroxine that is in excess; TSH is usually low.

questions.prompt: Why does glucose appear in the urine of a person with untreated type 1 diabetes?

options.B: Insulin is normally excreted with glucose
options.C: Kidney cells convert urea into glucose
options.D: So much glucose is filtered that the tubule cannot reabsorb all of it

questions.explanation: Reabsorption of glucose relies on carrier proteins that have a maximum rate. Very high blood glucose means more is filtered than can be taken back. Option A is backwards: glucose is filtered normally, which is how it gets into the urine at all.

questions.prompt: People with untreated type 1 diabetes often lose weight even though their blood glucose is high. Why?

options.A: Without insulin, body cells take up little glucose, so they break down fats and proteins for energy
options.B: Glucose in the blood is directly excreted through the skin
options.C: High blood glucose lowers metabolic rate
options.D: Too much glycogen is stored in the liver

questions.explanation: Insulin is needed for muscle and fat cells to take up glucose. Without it, cells are short of fuel and use fat and protein stores. Option D is wrong because without insulin the liver stores less glycogen, not more.

questions.prompt: In Graves' disease, thyroxine is high but TSH from the pituitary is low. Why does thyroxine stay high?

options.A: The pituitary has stopped responding to thyroxine
options.B: Antibodies activate TSH receptors on the thyroid, and these are not reduced by negative feedback
options.C: The thyroid has run out of iodine
options.D: The hypothalamus is producing too much TSH

questions.explanation: Low TSH shows negative feedback is working, but antibodies mimic TSH and keep stimulating the thyroid. Option A is tempting, but if the pituitary ignored thyroxine, TSH would be high, not low.

questions.prompt: A patient produces very large volumes of dilute urine. Injecting synthetic ADH has no effect. The most likely explanation is that

options.A: the hypothalamus is not making ADH
options.B: the pancreas is not making insulin
options.C: the collecting duct cells do not respond to ADH
options.D: the patient has too much ADH

questions.explanation: If extra ADH does nothing, the fault is at the target cells (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus). Option A, central diabetes insipidus, would improve with synthetic ADH, because the missing hormone would be replaced.

questions.prompt: A person with hyperthyroidism is likely to show which combination of symptoms?

options.A: Feeling cold, weight gain and slow heart rate
options.B: Feeling cold, weight loss and fast heart rate
options.C: Feeling hot, weight gain and slow heart rate
options.D: Feeling hot, weight loss and fast heart rate

questions.explanation: Excess thyroxine raises metabolic rate, so more heat is made, energy stores are used up faster and the heart beats faster. Option A describes hypothyroidism, the opposite condition.

questions.prompt: Two patients have high blood glucose. Patient 1 has very low insulin; patient 2 has high insulin. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Patient 1 likely has a beta cell fault; patient 2 likely has target cells that respond poorly to insulin
options.C: Patient 1 has insulin resistance; patient 2 has beta cell destruction
options.D: Both patients would respond equally well to insulin injections

questions.explanation: Low insulin with high glucose points to a gland fault (as in type 1); high insulin with high glucose points to target cells not responding (as in type 2). Option C reverses the two patients.
